meta.title: Natural Hazards & Society
meta.note: Every question tests concepts, mechanisms and their application. No question asks for dates, magnitudes, temperatures or other facts about particular disasters.

topics.name: How geoscientists study and monitor Earth
Plate tectonics as a unifying theory
Warnings & reducing earthquake and tsunami risk

questions.stem: A risk planner sorts hazards by the process that mainly causes them. Which classification follows the definitions in the notes?
options: A flood is a geohazard, because the water moves across the Earth's surface
A tropical cyclone is a geohazard, because it forms over the Earth's oceans
A landslide is a geohazard, while a heatwave is a natural hazard that is not a geohazard
A volcanic eruption is not a geohazard, because its ash plume is carried by the atmosphere
rationales: Floods arise mainly from hydrological processes, so the notes list them as natural hazards that are not geohazards. Moving across the surface is not the test.
Cyclones are driven by atmospheric circulation over warm oceans. Forming over the ocean does not make a hazard geological.
Correct. A geohazard is caused mainly by geological or Earth processes, such as a slope failing. A heatwave comes from atmospheric processes, so it is a natural hazard but not a geohazard.
The eruption is driven by processes inside the Earth, so it is a geohazard. The ash plume is a product of the eruption, not its cause.
questions.takeaway: Classify a hazard by the process that mainly drives it: geological processes make a geohazard; atmospheric, hydrological or biological ones do not.

questions.stem: Two towns are hit by floods of the same size. One suffers a disaster while the other sees only minor disruption. What best explains the difference?
options: Floods are not geohazards, so whether they cause disasters is largely a matter of luck
Only one town received a forecast, and forecasts alone remove the unequal impacts
The flood must have been physically larger in the town where the disaster happened
The flood became a disaster only where it struck an exposed and vulnerable society
rationales: Whether a hazard is a geohazard has nothing to do with whether it becomes a disaster. Exposure and vulnerability decide that, not luck.
The notes stress that scientific forecasts and monitoring alone cannot eliminate unequal impacts, so a forecast cannot be the full explanation.
The stem fixes the floods at the same size. The difference lies in the people and places affected, not the physical event.
Correct. A hazard becomes a disaster when it severely disrupts an exposed and vulnerable society. The same hazard can produce very different consequences for different people.
questions.takeaway: Hazard plus an exposed, vulnerable society makes a disaster; the same hazard can have very different outcomes.

questions.stem: A government spends its entire disaster budget on a world-class hazard monitoring network and nothing else. Based on the notes, what is the most likely outcome?
options: Disaster risk should fall to zero for monitored hazards, since their timing will always be known well in advance
Unequal impacts are likely to remain, since risk reduction also needs policy, emergency management and communities
Unequal impacts should largely disappear, since better forecasts will reach every community in the same way
Disadvantaged communities should recover the fastest, since they gain the most from the new scientific data
rationales: Monitoring improves understanding, but it does not remove exposure or vulnerability, so risk cannot fall to zero.
Correct. Forecasts and monitoring alone cannot eliminate unequal impacts. Reducing disaster risk needs science, policy, emergency management and communities working together.
Better forecasts do not change where people live, building quality, wealth or access to support, which shape exposure and vulnerability.
The notes say disadvantaged communities are often more exposed, less prepared and slower to recover. Data alone does not reverse that.
questions.takeaway: Monitoring is necessary but not sufficient: disaster risk reduction needs science, policy, emergency management and communities together.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the factors the notes list as shaping a community's exposure and vulnerability?
options: The physical size of the hazard event that strikes the area
Where people live relative to the places the hazard reaches
The quality of buildings and the infrastructure people use
Household wealth and how much outside support people can get
rationales: Correct. The size of the event describes the hazard itself. Exposure and vulnerability are about the society the hazard meets.
Where people live is listed as a key factor: it decides who is exposed to the hazard in the first place.
Building quality and infrastructure are listed factors. They decide how well people withstand the hazard.
Wealth and access to support are listed factors. They affect how well people prepare and how fast they recover.
questions.takeaway: Exposure and vulnerability describe the society (location, buildings, wealth, infrastructure, support), not the size of the hazard.

questions.stem: Two neighbourhoods feel the same earthquake shaking. Months later, the poorer neighbourhood is still struggling while the wealthier one has largely recovered. Which statement best explains this?
options: The shaking must have been stronger in the poorer area, which is why recovery took longer there
Wealthier areas always suffer more damage, so they receive more help and recover sooner
Recovery speed depends only on the hazard, so the difference must have come down to chance
Disadvantaged communities are often less prepared and have less support, so recovery is slower
rationales: The stem says both felt the same shaking. The difference comes from the communities, not the hazard.
Wealthier areas may lose more in value, but the notes link wealth with better preparation and faster recovery, not with more damage.
Recovery depends heavily on wealth, infrastructure and access to support, so the difference is not chance.
Correct. The notes say disadvantaged communities are often more exposed, less prepared and slower to recover. The same hazard produces different consequences for different people.
questions.takeaway: Inequality in exposure, preparation and support makes the same hazard hit disadvantaged communities harder and for longer.

questions.stem: The notes say that natural hazards have unnatural impacts. What does this mean?
options: The physical processes behind most hazards are poorly understood and so seem unnatural
The harm a hazard causes depends largely on how society is organised and where people live
Natural hazards only cause harm when scientists fail to forecast them in time for people
Most natural hazards are now triggered by human activities rather than by the Earth's processes
rationales: The phrase is about impacts on society, not about how well scientists understand the physical processes.
Correct. A natural hazard becomes a disaster through its interaction with people and society, so its impacts are shaped by human factors.
Forecasts cannot eliminate unequal impacts, so harm does not depend only on whether a forecast was made.
The hazards themselves are still natural processes. The unnatural part is how their impacts are distributed across society.
questions.takeaway: The hazard is natural; the size and spread of its impacts are shaped by society.

questions.stem: Two hazards differ enormously in how large an area they affect and how long they last. According to the notes, which aspects does this difference in scale shape?
options: How often they recur, their impacts, and how we monitor, prepare for and mitigate them
Whether each hazard should be counted as a natural hazard or as one caused by humans
Whether each hazard is a geohazard, with larger ones always counted as weather hazards
Only how often each hazard happens, since all hazards are monitored in the same way
rationales: Correct. Hazards operate across many orders of magnitude in space and time, and this shapes their recurrence, intensity and impacts, how they interact, and how we measure, monitor, prepare and mitigate.
Scale does not decide whether a hazard is natural. Both small and very large hazards can be natural processes.
Classification as a geohazard depends on the process involved, not on size. Earthquakes are geohazards at every size.
Scale affects much more than frequency, including how hazards are measured and monitored, so they are not all monitored the same way.
questions.takeaway: A hazard's spatial and temporal scale shapes its frequency, impacts, interactions and how we monitor and manage it.

questions.stem: Why do geoscientists bring together many disciplines when studying the Earth and its hazards?
options: Numerical models have replaced fieldwork, so disciplines now mainly share computer code
Each discipline studies a separate layer of the Earth, so their findings never need to meet
No single discipline explains the whole Earth, so different perspectives must be combined
Geoscience is really one single field, and its sub-fields differ only in their instruments
rationales: Geoscientists still combine field observations, laboratory work, instruments, data and models. Models have not replaced fieldwork.
The disciplines overlap and depend on each other. Understanding Earth needs their findings to be combined.
Correct. Each discipline offers a different way to study Earth, and geoscience depends on bringing those perspectives together.
The notes describe many disciplines, each with a different way of studying Earth, not one field split only by instruments.
questions.takeaway: Geoscience works by combining disciplines, because no single one explains the whole Earth.

questions.stem: A geoscientist studies how a volcanic eruption sends ash into the atmosphere, which changes rainfall, which in turn triggers landslides on distant slopes. Which way of thinking is this?
options: Thinking about time, by placing the eruption on a scale of billions of years
Spatial thinking, by picturing the volcano and the slopes in three dimensions
Treating Earth as a complex system of interacting processes and feedbacks
Learning in the field, by using the volcano's rocks as the direct evidence
rationales: Thinking about time covers processes from seconds to billions of years, but this study is about linked processes, not long timescales.
Spatial thinking may help map the slopes, but the core of this study is the chain of linked processes, not the 3D picture.
Correct. Tracing how one process sets off others in the atmosphere and on land is examining interactions, feedbacks and connections in a complex Earth system.
Field evidence can support the study, but the reasoning described is about connections between processes.
questions.takeaway: Following a chain of linked processes across Earth's systems is systems thinking.

questions.stem: A student studies a map and a cross-section to picture how a sinking plate dips beneath a continent. Which way of thinking from the notes is the student using?
options: Spatial thinking: picturing Earth in three dimensions from maps and cross-sections
Thinking about time: following how processes unfold over seconds to billions of years
Systems thinking: tracing feedbacks and connections between different Earth processes
Learning in the field: using rocks and landscapes seen on site as the main evidence
rationales: Correct. Spatial thinking means visualising Earth in 3D and interpreting maps, cross-sections and spatial patterns.
The student is not working with timescales here. They are building a 3D picture from 2D sources.
No feedbacks between processes are involved; the task is purely about geometry in three dimensions.
The student is working from a map and cross-section, not from rocks observed in the field.
questions.takeaway: Reading maps and cross-sections to picture Earth in 3D is spatial thinking.

questions.stem: A developer argues that a fault is harmless because it has not produced an earthquake in recorded history. Which way of thinking from the notes best exposes the flaw?
options: Spatial thinking, since the fault must be mapped in three dimensions before anything is said
Thinking about time, since fault processes can span far longer than human records
Systems thinking, since a fault only matters through its feedbacks with the climate
Learning in the field, since only a rock sample can show whether the fault exists
rationales: Mapping helps, but the developer's error is about the length of the record, not about the geometry of the fault.
Correct. Geoscientists think about processes over timescales from seconds to billions of years. Recorded history is far too short to judge how often a fault ruptures.
A fault's hazard comes from its own slip, not from feedbacks with the climate.
Field evidence can help, but the flaw in the argument is the assumption that a short record captures the fault's behaviour.
questions.takeaway: Earth processes often run on timescales longer than human records, so silence in history does not mean safety.

questions.stem: A team must assess the hazard from an unfamiliar fault. Which plan best reflects how the notes say geoscientists build understanding?
options: Run a numerical model first, then skip fieldwork if the model output looks realistic enough to trust
Collect field observations only, since rocks and landscapes record everything that happened
Install instruments only, since present-day data alone show how the fault behaved in the past
Map the fault in the field, analyse samples, record it with instruments and test ideas in models
rationales: Models are one tool among several. Skipping fieldwork removes the evidence the model should be tested against.
Field observations are valuable, but on their own they leave out lab analysis, instruments and modelling.
Present-day instruments capture recent behaviour only. The fault's longer history needs field and laboratory evidence.
Correct. Geoscientists combine field observations, laboratory analyses, instruments, data and numerical models to understand Earth and assess hazards.
questions.takeaway: Hazard assessment combines field, laboratory, instrument and model evidence.

questions.stem: Why is plate tectonics described as a unifying theory?
options: It explains why earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain belts occur where they do
It explains every natural hazard, including floods, cyclones and heatwaves
It is the one theory that geoscientists from every discipline agree upon
It unifies the continents, which were all joined into one landmass long ago
rationales: Correct. Plate tectonics explains how Earth's surface changes and why earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain belts occur where they do, giving a common framework for many geohazards.
Floods, cyclones and heatwaves are not geohazards. They arise from atmospheric and hydrological processes, which plate tectonics does not explain.
Agreement among scientists is not what makes it unifying. It is unifying because it explains many different features with one framework.
Past continental positions are part of the evidence for the theory, not the reason it is called unifying.
questions.takeaway: Plate tectonics unifies by explaining the distribution of earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain belts within one framework.

questions.stem: A world map shows that most earthquakes and volcanoes fall in long, narrow belts rather than being spread evenly. What is the best explanation?
options: They follow the coastlines, where continental and ocean crust always meet each other
Most of them occur along plate boundaries, where moving plates interact
They lie above the hottest parts of the core, which melt the crust above
They mark the places where the Earth's crust is thickest and heaviest
rationales: Many coastlines have few earthquakes, and many belts run through the middle of oceans. The belts follow plate boundaries.
Correct. Plate tectonics explains why earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated where plates diverge, converge or slide past each other.
The core does not melt the crust directly, and the belts follow plate boundaries rather than hot spots in the core.
Crustal thickness alone does not explain the belts. Many belts lie along mid-ocean ridges, where the crust is thin.
questions.takeaway: Earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along plate boundaries, which is what plate tectonics predicts.

questions.stem: A student claims that plate motion is far too slow to measure, so it can only be inferred from ancient rocks. Which response is best?
options: The claim is right, because plates only move during the brief seconds of large earthquakes
The claim is right, because plate motion stopped once the ancient continents broke apart
Plate motion can be measured, but only from space by tracking entire continents at once
Plate motion can be measured directly, using GPS over a few years or offsets across faults
rationales: Plates move steadily between earthquakes too. The fault may be locked, but the plates keep moving.
Plates are still moving today. That is why GPS stations record steady changes in position.
Ground-based evidence such as fault offsets works too, and GPS stations sit on the ground rather than tracking whole continents.
Correct. Plate motion can be measured directly: offsets along faults show it over years, and GPS records smaller movements over shorter periods.
questions.takeaway: Plate motion is measurable today, with GPS over years and with fault offsets.

questions.stem: Fossils of the same distinctive land species are found on two continents that are now separated by a wide ocean. What does this most directly suggest?
options: Ocean currents carried the fossils from one continent to the other
Sea level was once low enough to expose the whole ocean floor
The two continents were once joined and have since drifted apart
The same species evolved separately on each continent by chance
rationales: These are land species preserved in rock where they lived. Currents do not move fossils between continents.
The ocean floor is far too deep to have been exposed by a fall in sea level. Continental drift is the explanation the notes give.
Correct. Matching fossils across an ocean was one of Wegener's observations of continental drift, and plate tectonics explains it: the continents were once together.
The same distinctive species arising separately on two continents is very unlikely. Joined continents explain the match far more simply.
questions.takeaway: Matching fossils on continents now separated by ocean are evidence that the continents were once joined.

questions.stem: Some evidence for plate tectonics shows where continents were in the past; other evidence shows how plates move today. Which observation belongs to the second kind?
options: Magnetic stripes on the ocean floor recording past reversals of the field
Matching fossils found on continents now separated by an ocean
Glacial scratches that line up once the continents are fitted together
GPS stations recording steady shifts in position over several years
rationales: Magnetic stripes record spreading that happened over long spans of time, which is evidence about the past.
Fossils record where continents were when the organisms lived, which is evidence about the past.
Glacial striations show continents were once attached near a common point, which is evidence about the past.
Correct. GPS measures present-day plate motion directly, over periods of just a few years.
questions.takeaway: Fossils, striations and stripes record past motion; GPS measures motion today.

questions.stem: A large earthquake strikes an uninhabited desert with no buildings or infrastructure. How should it be described?
options: As a disaster, because geohazards are disasters by definition, unlike weather hazards
As a hazard event but not a disaster, as no exposed and vulnerable society was disrupted
As neither, because only earthquakes near plate boundaries can count as natural hazards
As a disaster, because any earthquake large enough to be recorded automatically counts as one
rationales: Geohazards are a category of natural hazard, and like any hazard they only become disasters when they disrupt society.
Correct. A hazard becomes a disaster only when it severely disrupts an exposed and vulnerable society. With nobody exposed, it remains a hazard event.
Earthquakes within plates are still natural hazards. Location relative to a boundary does not decide whether something is a hazard.
Size alone does not make a disaster. The test is how much it disrupts an exposed, vulnerable society.
questions.takeaway: No exposed, vulnerable society means no disaster, however large the hazard.

questions.stem: Which description best fits a natural hazard that is NOT a geohazard?
options: One arising from geological processes but made noticeably worse by human activity
One whose effects are felt mostly at sea rather than on dry land
One arising mainly from atmospheric, hydrological or biological processes
One that unfolds too slowly to be detected by monitoring instruments
rationales: If the hazard arises from geological processes it is still a geohazard, whatever humans add.
A tsunami acts mainly at the coast and sea yet is a geohazard. Where effects are felt does not decide the category.
Correct. Non-geohazards are linked to weather, climate, water or biological systems rather than Earth's geological activity.
Speed and detectability are not part of the definition. The category depends on the process causing the hazard.
questions.takeaway: Non-geohazards come from atmospheric, hydrological or biological processes.

questions.stem: Under the classification in the notes, how should an epidemic be described?
options: A natural hazard arising from biological processes, so not a geohazard
Not a natural hazard at all, since it does not involve Earth processes
A weather-related hazard, since outbreaks are driven by the climate
A geohazard, since the disease spreads from place to place across the Earth's surface
rationales: Correct. Epidemics and pandemics are listed as biological hazards: natural hazards that are not geohazards.
Natural hazards include atmospheric, hydrological and biological processes, not only Earth processes. An epidemic still counts.
The notes classify epidemics as biological hazards, not weather-related ones.
Spreading across the surface does not make something geological. Geohazards arise from Earth's internal or surface processes.
questions.takeaway: Epidemics are biological natural hazards, not geohazards.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the lithosphere with the asthenosphere?
options: The lithosphere is the crust alone; the asthenosphere is the molten outer core lying beneath it
The lithosphere is defined by its composition, while the asthenosphere is defined by its depth alone
The lithosphere is rigid crust plus uppermost mantle; the asthenosphere below is hotter and weaker
The lithosphere is weak and slowly flowing; the asthenosphere is the rigid shell carrying the plates
rationales: The lithosphere includes the uppermost mantle as well as the crust, and the asthenosphere is part of the upper mantle, not the outer core.
Both are described by how they behave: rigid versus hotter and weaker. Crust, mantle and core are the layers defined by composition.
Correct. The lithosphere is the solid, rigid outer shell made of the crust and uppermost mantle, forming the plates. It sits on the hotter, weaker asthenosphere, which deforms slowly.
This reverses the two layers. The rigid lithosphere forms the plates; the weaker asthenosphere beneath deforms slowly and lets them move.
questions.takeaway: Lithosphere = rigid crust + uppermost mantle (the plates); asthenosphere = hotter, weaker upper mantle beneath.

questions.stem: Suppose the asthenosphere were as rigid as the lithosphere above it. What would most directly follow for plate motion?
options: Nothing would change, since plates are carried along by the outer core, not the mantle
Plates would struggle to move, since the weak layer that lets them glide would be gone
Plates would move faster, since a rigid layer passes slab pull on more efficiently
Plates would still move, but only at the moment large earthquakes rupture their edges
rationales: Plates ride on the asthenosphere in the upper mantle. The outer core is far deeper and does not carry the plates.
Correct. The asthenosphere's ability to deform slowly is what allows the plates above it to move. Remove that weakness and plate motion would be resisted.
Slab pull needs the plate to move over a weaker layer. A rigid layer below would resist the motion rather than help it.
Plates move steadily, not only during earthquakes. Earthquakes are sudden releases of strain built up by that steady motion.
questions.takeaway: Plates can move because the asthenosphere beneath them is hot and weak enough to deform slowly.

questions.stem: Which description of mantle convection is accurate?
options: Solid mantle flows slowly over geological time, with hot, less dense rock rising and cool rock sinking
Liquid mantle circulates only beneath mid-ocean ridges and stays completely still everywhere else
Molten mantle flows rapidly under the plates, with hot, dense rock rising and cool, light rock sinking
Solid mantle stays fixed in place, and heat leaves the interior only through volcanoes at the surface
rationales: Correct. Heat escaping from Earth's interior lets the solid mantle deform and flow slowly over geological time; hotter, less dense mantle rises and cooler, denser material sinks.
The mantle is not liquid, and convection is not confined to ridges.
The mantle is solid and flows very slowly. Hot material rises because it is less dense, not denser.
The mantle is not fixed: it deforms and flows slowly, and convection carries heat out of the interior.
questions.takeaway: Mantle convection: solid rock flowing slowly, with hot, less dense rock rising and cool, dense rock sinking.

questions.stem: According to the notes, what is the main force driving plate motion, and where does it act?
options: Rising hot mantle beneath mid-ocean ridges, which lifts the plates and pushes them outward
The weight of high mountain belts, which presses the plates down and squeezes them sideways
Drag from the spinning liquid outer core, which turns the whole mantle and the plates above
Slab pull, where cold, dense oceanic lithosphere sinks into the mantle at subduction zones
rationales: Hot mantle does rise, but the notes identify the sinking slab at subduction zones as the main driver.
Mountain belts are a result of plate collision, not the force that drives plates.
The outer core produces the magnetic field. It does not drag the mantle and plates along.
Correct. At subduction zones, cold oceanic lithosphere sinks and pulls the rest of the plate with it. The notes call this slab pull, the main driving force of plate motion.
questions.takeaway: Slab pull, the sinking of cold, dense oceanic lithosphere at subduction zones, is the main driver of plate motion.

questions.stem: A student lists crust, mantle, outer core and inner core alongside lithosphere and asthenosphere. What distinguishes the first set from the second?
options: The first set describes the oceans; the second set describes the continents
The first set is used for earthquakes; the second set is used for volcanoes
The first is defined by composition; the second by how rigid or weak the rock is
The first set is solid all the way through; the second set is entirely molten
rationales: Both sets apply under oceans and continents alike. They describe Earth's layers, not types of surface.
Both sets are used throughout geoscience. They differ in what defines the layers, not in which hazard they explain.
Correct. Crust, mantle, outer core and inner core are defined by composition. The lithosphere is the rigid outer shell and the asthenosphere the hotter, weaker layer beneath it.
The outer core is liquid, and the asthenosphere is solid but weak. Neither set is all solid or all molten.
questions.takeaway: Crust/mantle/core are compositional layers; lithosphere/asthenosphere are defined by rigid versus weak behaviour.

questions.stem: A research ship samples seafloor rock at increasing distances from a mid-ocean ridge, on both sides of it. What pattern should the ages show?
options: Ages are similar everywhere, since the floor formed at once
Ages increase away from the ridge, mirrored on both sides
Ages increase away from the ridge, but only on one side
Ages decrease away from the ridge, mirrored on both sides
rationales: Ocean crust forms continuously at ridges, so its age varies systematically with distance.
Correct. New crust forms at the ridge, so rock nearest the ridge is youngest and gets older with distance. Spreading on both sides gives a mirrored pattern.
Spreading happens on both sides of the ridge, so the age pattern is symmetrical, not one-sided.
This reverses the pattern. The ridge is where new material emerges, so the youngest rock is there.
questions.takeaway: Ocean floor is youngest at the ridge and older with distance, symmetrically on both sides.

questions.stem: Why is the pattern of magnetic stripes on one side of a mid-ocean ridge a mirror image of the pattern on the other side?
options: Erosion wears both sides of the ridge at the same rate, smoothing them into matching stripes
The magnetic field is strongest at the ridge, so the stripes fade evenly in both directions
Reversals start beneath the ridge and travel outward through the crust on both sides
New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides, recording the same reversals
rationales: The stripes are a magnetic record frozen into the rock, not a product of erosion.
Stripes record alternating polarity, not a fading strength, and field strength is not what makes them symmetrical.
Reversals are flips of the whole field generated in the core. They do not travel outward through the crust.
Correct. Crust forming at the ridge is split and carried away on both sides, so each reversal is recorded in matching bands either side.
questions.takeaway: Symmetrical stripes form because crust made at the ridge spreads away on both sides while recording each reversal.

questions.stem: Why do the magnetic minerals in ocean crust preserve the direction of Earth's field at the time the crust formed?
options: They align with the field while the rock is hot, then are frozen in place as it cools
They keep realigning with the field throughout the rock's life, recording the latest polarity
They can only align once the rock is cold, so they record the field long after eruption
They align with the direction of plate motion, which changes each time the ridge shifts
rationales: Correct. Magnetic particles can move to align with the field only while the rock is hot. Once it cools, their orientation is locked in.
If the minerals kept realigning, all the crust would show today's polarity and there would be no stripes.
This reverses the timing. The particles can move only while hot and are frozen once the rock cools.
The minerals align with Earth's magnetic field, like a compass needle, not with the direction of plate motion.
questions.takeaway: Hot rock lets magnetic minerals align with the field; cooling locks that direction in.

questions.stem: Imagine Earth's magnetic field had never reversed, but seafloor spreading worked exactly as it does today. What would the ocean floor show?
options: Uniform magnetization with no stripes, even though crust still spread from the ridge
No new crust at all, because spreading at the ridge depends on the field reversing
Stripes would still form, but they would run across the ridge instead of parallel to it
Stripes would still form, because spreading alone creates bands of alternating polarity
rationales: Correct. Stripes record alternating polarity. Without reversals all the crust would be magnetized the same way, even though spreading continued.
Spreading is driven by plate motion and rising magma, not by the magnetic field. Crust would still form.
Without reversals there would be no alternating bands to run in any direction.
Spreading carries the record away from the ridge, but the alternation itself comes from reversals of the field.
questions.takeaway: Spreading moves the record away from the ridge; reversals create the alternating stripes.

questions.stem: Which description of the magnetic stripes on the ocean floor is fully correct?
options: Parallel to the ridge, all of one polarity, symmetrical on either side of it
Parallel to the ridge, alternating in polarity, symmetrical on either side
Parallel to the ridge, alternating in polarity, offset on one side only
At right angles to the ridge, alternating in polarity, symmetrical either side
rationales: The stripes alternate in polarity; that alternation is what makes them stripes.
Correct. The three key features are that the stripes are parallel to the ridge, alternate in polarity and form a symmetrical pattern.
The pattern is symmetrical either side of the ridge, because spreading carries crust away on both sides.
The stripes run parallel to the ridge, because each band forms along the ridge at the time it was active.
questions.takeaway: Magnetic stripes are parallel to the ridge, alternating and symmetrical.

questions.stem: Where does Earth's magnetic field, whose reversals are recorded in the ocean floor, come from?
options: Magnetic minerals in the crust, which together act like one very large bar magnet
The solid inner core, which spins in one direction and then reverses its rotation
Convection in the solid mantle, which drags magnetized plates around the planet
Convection and rotation of the liquid iron-nickel outer core, forming a geodynamo
rationales: Crustal minerals record the field; they do not generate it.
The notes place the geodynamo in the liquid outer core, not in a spinning solid inner core.
Mantle convection moves the plates, but the field is generated in the liquid outer core.
Correct. Convection and rotation of the conductive liquid outer core create the geodynamo, a self-sustaining field that can flip polarity.
questions.takeaway: The geodynamo in the liquid outer core generates Earth's magnetic field, which can flip polarity.

questions.stem: Rock on the ocean floor is generally much younger than many continental rocks. What best explains this?
options: The continents formed first, and oceans only began spreading in recent geological time
Seawater erodes ocean rock away quickly, so only the youngest rock stays exposed on the floor
Old oceanic lithosphere is returned to the mantle at subduction zones, which continents avoid
Each magnetic reversal resets the age of ocean rock, so its measured age always looks young
rationales: Spreading has gone on throughout geological time. The ocean floor is young because it is constantly destroyed and replaced.
Ocean crust is not lost through erosion; it is recycled into the mantle at subduction zones.

Correct. Ocean crust forms at ridges and is destroyed at subduction zones, because dense oceanic plates sink. Continental crust is less dense and is not recycled the same way, so it can be much older.
Reversals are recorded in the rock's magnetism. They do not change its age.
questions.takeaway: Ocean floor stays young because it is made at ridges and destroyed at subduction zones.

questions.stem: Why do ridges form along divergent plate boundaries?
options: The plates pull apart, opening space for magma to rise, cool and build new crust
The plates push together, buckling the crust upward into a long submarine ridge
One plate sinks under the other, and the melted slab rises to build up a ridge
The plates slide past each other, piling up crust where their edges grind together
rationales: Correct. At divergent boundaries the plates move apart, and the space is filled by new crust formed from magma rising and cooling, building a ridge.
Pushing together describes convergent boundaries, which produce trenches and mountain belts rather than spreading ridges.
Sinking of one plate under another describes subduction at convergent boundaries, which forms trenches.
Sliding past each other describes transform boundaries, where crust is neither created nor destroyed.
questions.takeaway: Ridges mark divergent boundaries, where plates separate and magma fills the gap with new crust.

questions.stem: A long valley on a continent is slowly widening, with frequent shallow earthquakes and volcanic activity. If the process continues, what is the likely long-term outcome?
options: It will close into a mountain belt once the two sides begin to subduct together
It will turn into a transform boundary once the valley stops getting any wider
It will become a deep-ocean trench as the valley floor sinks into the mantle
It may open into a new ocean basin as the divergent boundary keeps spreading
rationales: A widening valley shows the plates moving apart. Mountain belts form where plates converge.
A transform boundary involves sliding past, not a pause in spreading. Nothing in the setting points to that change.
Trenches form where one plate subducts beneath another at a convergent boundary, not in a widening rift.
Correct. On land a divergent boundary produces a rift, which can eventually open up and become an ocean basin.
questions.takeaway: A continental rift is a divergent boundary on land that can grow into an ocean basin.

questions.stem: An oceanic plate converges with a continental plate. Which one subducts, and why?
options: The continental plate, because it is thicker and so heavier than the oceanic plate
The oceanic plate, because it is denser even though the continental plate is thicker
Neither, because plates of different types slide past each other at a transform
Whichever plate is moving faster, regardless of its density or its thickness
rationales: Thickness does not decide it. The continental plate is thicker but less dense, so it stays on top.
Correct. The denser oceanic plate is subducted beneath the less dense plate. Continental plates are thicker, but density is what decides which one sinks.
Converging plates collide; sliding past describes transform boundaries.
Speed is not what decides which plate sinks. Density is.
questions.takeaway: Oceanic plates are denser, continental plates thicker; the denser plate subducts.

questions.stem: Two continents converge after all the ocean floor between them has subducted. What is expected to happen?
options: A ridge forms between them as magma rises into the gap left by the subducted ocean
The thicker continent subducts, forming a deep trench and a chain of volcanoes above
Neither sinks easily, so the crust shortens and thickens into a high mountain range
The plates stop moving at once, because two continents cannot interact with each other
rationales: Ridges form where plates move apart, but here the plates are converging.
Continental crust is less dense and resists subduction. Thickness does not make it sink.
Correct. Collision starts as ocean subducting under a continent, but continental material arriving behind it does not sink easily, so the crust thickens into mountains such as the Himalayas.
The plates keep converging; the motion is taken up by shortening and thickening the crust.
questions.takeaway: Continent-continent collision builds high mountains because neither continent sinks easily.

questions.stem: Which description fits a transform plate boundary?
options: Plates move apart horizontally, and new crust is created to fill the opening gap
Plates slide horizontally past each other, and crust is neither created nor destroyed
Plates slide past each other, and crust is destroyed as one edge is ground away
Plates collide horizontally, and crust is created as the colliding edges fold up
rationales: Moving apart and creating crust describes a divergent boundary.
Correct. At transform boundaries the relative motion is horizontal, they can be on land or underwater, and crust is neither destroyed nor created.
Sliding past is right, but crust is not destroyed at transform boundaries.
Collision describes convergent boundaries, and those destroy crust rather than create it.
questions.takeaway: Transform boundary: horizontal sliding past, with no crust created or destroyed.

questions.stem: On a detailed map of a mid-ocean ridge, many short faults cut across the ridge and offset it into segments. What are these faults?
options: Transform boundaries, where ridge segments are linked by plates sliding past
Normal faults, where crust at the ridge is pulled downward into a rift valley
Collision zones, where two ridge segments push into each other and buckle up
Small subduction zones, where the youngest crust sinks back into the mantle
rationales: Correct. Transform faults connect segments of mid-ocean ridges, letting the plates slide past each other between them.
Normal faults run along the ridge as it pulls apart. Faults cutting across and offsetting the ridge are transforms.
Ridge segments are spreading apart, not colliding.
The youngest crust is at the ridge and is too buoyant to subduct there. Subduction happens far away at trenches.
questions.takeaway: Transform faults link and offset segments of mid-ocean ridges.

questions.stem: Beneath one region, earthquakes get steadily deeper in one direction, tracing a sloping band into the mantle. What does this indicate?
options: A hotspot, with earthquakes tracking the path of the mantle plume beneath it
A divergent boundary, with magma rising from deeper levels as plates separate
A transform boundary, with faults reaching deeper the further from the ridge
A subducting slab, with earthquakes following it as it sinks into the mantle
rationales: A hotspot plume rises roughly vertically and does not produce a sloping band of deep earthquakes.
Earthquakes at divergent boundaries are shallow. They do not trace a deep sloping band.
Transform earthquakes are shallow and do not form a band sloping into the mantle.
Correct. This sloping zone of earthquakes, the Wadati-Benioff zone, follows the subducting slab. It is why the deepest earthquakes occur along subduction zones.
questions.takeaway: A sloping band of deepening earthquakes (Wadati-Benioff zone) traces a subducting slab.

questions.stem: Which pairing of landform with plate boundary type is fully correct?
options: Trench: convergent; ridge: transform; fault offsetting a ridge: divergent
Trench: transform; ridge: divergent; fault offsetting a ridge: convergent
Trench: convergent; ridge: divergent; fault offsetting a ridge: transform
Trench: divergent; ridge: convergent; fault offsetting a ridge: transform
rationales: Ridges form at divergent boundaries, and the faults that offset them are transforms.
Trenches form at convergent boundaries where one plate subducts, not at transforms.
Correct. Trenches form where plates converge and one subducts, ridges form where plates diverge, and faults offsetting a ridge are transforms.
Trenches and ridges are swapped. Ridges form where plates move apart.
questions.takeaway: Trench → convergent; ridge → divergent; ridge-offsetting fault → transform.

questions.stem: Which sequence follows elastic rebound theory?
options: The plates stop moving, the fault cools and shrinks, and the rock cracks to make waves
Strain builds suddenly at a fault, is released slowly over decades, and the rock stays bent
Strain builds slowly near a locked fault, is released suddenly as slip, and the rock rebounds
Magma forces the fault open, heat escapes as seismic waves, and the rock melts and resets
rationales: The plates keep moving; it is the locked fault that stores strain until it slips.
This reverses the timing. Strain builds slowly over decades and is released suddenly.
Correct. Elastic deformation accumulates slowly from plate motion, the stored stress is suddenly released as an earthquake, and the rocks rebound so the next cycle can start.
Elastic rebound involves stored elastic stress in rock, not magma or melting.
questions.takeaway: Elastic rebound: slow strain build-up, sudden release, rocks rebound, and the cycle repeats.

questions.stem: Bending a stick of dry pasta until it snaps is used as an analogy for an earthquake. Which part of the earthquake process matches the moment of the snap?
options: The sudden release of stored elastic stress as the fault slips
The arrival of surface waves long after the main shaking
The slow build-up of strain as plate motion bends the rocks
The rocks returning to their bent shape once stress is gone
rationales: Correct. The snap is the sudden failure that releases stored stress, which on a fault is the earthquake.
Wave arrivals are a consequence of the rupture, not the failure itself.
That matches bending the pasta before it breaks, not the snap itself.
After the earthquake the rocks rebound towards their original, unbent shape, not a bent one.
questions.takeaway: An earthquake is the sudden failure that releases stress stored during slow loading.

questions.stem: How does a seismometer record the motion of the ground during an earthquake?
options: It measures the heat released by the fault as seismic waves pass beneath the station
Its suspended mass stays nearly still by inertia while the ground moves around it
It detects sound in the air, which arrives before the ground itself starts to move
Its suspended mass moves with the ground, and the change in its weight is recorded
rationales: Seismometers record ground motion, not heat.
Correct. Seismometers work on the inertial principle: the ground moves while the suspended mass does not, and the relative motion is recorded.
Seismometers record motion of the ground itself, not sound in the air.
If the mass moved with the ground there would be no relative motion to record. Its inertia is the point.
questions.takeaway: A seismometer records ground motion relative to an inertial suspended mass.

questions.stem: A seismometer far from an earthquake records a small first arrival followed later by a much larger arrival. Which interpretation is correct?
options: S waves arrived first with smaller amplitude; P waves followed with larger amplitude
Surface waves arrived first; P waves followed once they had climbed to the surface
P and S waves arrived together; the larger arrival was the ground's own echo
P waves arrived first with smaller amplitude; S waves followed with larger amplitude
rationales: This reverses the two body waves. P waves arrive first and are smaller.
Surface waves are the slowest and arrive after the body waves.
P waves travel faster than S waves, so they arrive at different times, and the gap grows with distance.
Correct. P waves are fastest so arrive first, with smaller amplitude. S waves are slower but larger and more destructive.
questions.takeaway: P waves arrive first and are smaller; S waves arrive later and shake harder.

questions.stem: A station records clear P waves but no S waves from an earthquake whose waves took a path deep through Earth's interior. What does this suggest about the path?
options: It crossed a solid layer, since P waves cannot pass through liquids
It crossed the lithosphere, where S waves are turned into P waves
It crossed only the crust, where S waves are too slow to be recorded
It crossed a liquid layer, since S waves cannot pass through liquids
rationales: P waves do pass through liquids. It is S waves that cannot.
S waves are not converted into P waves in the lithosphere. Their absence points to liquid on the path.
S waves are slower than P waves but still recorded through the crust. A deep path is the clue here.
Correct. S waves travel only through solids, while P waves travel through solids, liquids and gases. Losing the S waves points to a liquid layer such as the outer core.
questions.takeaway: S waves travel only through solids, so missing S waves reveal liquid along the path.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches properties to the two body waves?
options: P: fastest, with the largest amplitude; S: slower, smaller, passes through liquids
P: fastest, passes through solids, liquids and gases; S: slower, larger, solids only
P: slower but with the largest amplitude; S: fastest, smaller, passes through solids
P: slower, solids only; S: fastest, smaller, passes through solids, liquids and gases
rationales: P waves are fastest, but they have the smaller amplitude, and S waves cannot travel through liquids.
Correct. P waves are fastest, smaller and travel through solids, liquids and gases. S waves are slower, larger and travel only through solids.
P waves are the fastest wave, and S waves are slower and larger.
This swaps the properties of the two waves.
questions.takeaway: P: fast, small, any medium. S: slower, larger, solids only.

questions.stem: A building on the surface and a deep tunnel directly below it feel the same distant earthquake. Why would surface-wave shaking be stronger in the building?
options: Surface waves form at the free surface and their amplitude decays rapidly with depth
Surface waves travel only through liquids, so they speed up near the groundwater
Surface waves are the fastest waves, so they reach the surface before the tunnel
Surface waves are reflected P waves, which grow stronger the deeper they travel
rationales: Correct. Surface waves form at the free surface and their amplitude decays exponentially with depth, so the tunnel feels much less of them.
Surface waves travel along the ground, not only through liquids.
Surface waves are the slowest waves, not the fastest.
The notes describe surface waves forming at the free surface and weakening with depth, not strengthening.
questions.takeaway: Surface-wave amplitude is largest at the surface and decays with depth.

questions.stem: Which matching of plate boundary to its most typical fault type is correct?
options: Divergent: normal faults; convergent: strike-slip; transform: reverse or thrust
Divergent: reverse faults; convergent: normal faults; transform: strike-slip
Divergent: normal faults; convergent: reverse or thrust; transform: strike-slip
Divergent: strike-slip; convergent: reverse or thrust; transform: normal faults
rationales: Convergence compresses the crust, which makes reverse or thrust faults, not strike-slip.
Normal and reverse faults are swapped. Divergence pulls crust apart, which makes normal faults.
Correct. Pulling apart makes normal faults, compression makes reverse or thrust faults, and sliding past makes strike-slip faults.
Strike-slip faults belong at transform boundaries, where plates slide past horizontally.
questions.takeaway: Divergent → normal; convergent → reverse/thrust; transform → strike-slip.

questions.stem: Standing on one side of a strike-slip fault, you see that a fence crossing it has been offset so the far section has moved to your right. You walk across and look back. Which way has the section on your original side moved?
options: To the left, so the fault is left-lateral when viewed from that side
To the right as well, so the fault is right-lateral from both sides
Upward, because strike-slip offset looks vertical from the other side
Not at all, because only one block of a strike-slip fault ever moves
rationales: Lateral sense does not flip when you cross the fault. Both blocks are seen moving to the right of the observer.
Correct. Whichever side you stand on, the opposite block appears to have moved the same way, so a right-lateral fault looks right-lateral from both sides.
Strike-slip motion is horizontal from every viewpoint.
Offset is relative motion between two blocks; it looks the same from either side.
questions.takeaway: Right- or left-lateral is judged by how the opposite block moved, and it is the same from either side.

questions.stem: Which describes the motion on a normal fault?
options: The footwall moves down relative to the hanging wall as the crust is pulled apart
The hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall as the crust is squeezed together
The hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall as the crust is pulled apart
The two blocks slide sideways past each other with no vertical motion between them
rationales: If the footwall moves down relative to the hanging wall, the hanging wall has moved up. That is reverse motion, which does not fit pulling apart.
Hanging wall moving up under compression describes a reverse or thrust fault.
Correct. On a normal fault the block above the fault (hanging wall) moves down relative to the block below, as tectonic forces pull the crust apart.
Sideways motion with no vertical component describes a strike-slip fault.
questions.takeaway: Normal fault: hanging wall moves down, crust pulled apart.

questions.stem: A straight running track crosses a fault that ruptures as a reverse (thrust) fault. Measured along the ground afterwards, what has happened to the length of the track?
options: It is shorter, because compression pushed one block up and over the other
It is longer, because the hanging wall dropped down and away from the footwall
It is longer, because compression stretched the ground as the block was raised
It is the same, because thrust faults only move the blocks straight up and down
rationales: Correct. Reverse or thrust faults are caused by compression and result in shortening, so the track across the fault ends up shorter.
A hanging wall dropping away describes a normal fault, which lengthens the ground.
Compression shortens the crust; it does not stretch it.
Thrust motion carries one block up and over the other, which shortens the distance across the fault.
questions.takeaway: Reverse or thrust faulting shortens the ground across the fault.

questions.stem: Why can a blind thrust fault be especially hard to plan for?
options: It slips so slowly that it never stores enough strain for a damaging event
It only produces S waves, which seismometers cannot pick up at the surface
It lies only beneath the oceans, far away from any monitoring network
It slips without breaking the surface, so it is often unknown until it ruptures
rationales: Blind thrusts can produce damaging earthquakes; being hidden does not mean being harmless.
Blind thrusts produce the usual seismic waves, and seismometers record S waves.
Blind thrust faults occur on land too. What makes them hard to plan for is that they leave no surface trace.
Correct. A blind thrust slips but never breaks the surface, so it typically is not known until an earthquake happens.
questions.takeaway: Blind thrusts are dangerous because they leave no surface trace before they rupture.

questions.stem: A fault rupture shows both vertical offset and horizontal sliding along the same fault. How is this fault classified?
options: Normal fault, combining downward motion with sideways stretching
Blind thrust fault, combining hidden reverse motion with surface slip
Transform fault, combining spreading at a ridge with strike-slip motion
Oblique fault, combining normal or reverse motion with strike-slip motion
rationales: A normal fault is dip-slip; horizontal sliding along the fault makes it oblique.
A blind thrust does not break the surface at all, so it cannot show surface offset.
A transform is a strike-slip plate boundary. It does not combine vertical and horizontal motion in this way.
Correct. An oblique fault combines normal or reverse faulting with strike-slip motion.
questions.takeaway: Oblique fault = dip-slip (normal or reverse) plus strike-slip.

questions.stem: Which statement about the faults found at subduction zones is most accurate?
options: Strike-slip faults dominate, since the plates slide past each other at trenches
Only reverse or thrust faults can occur, since all motion there is compressional
Reverse or thrust faults are most expected, but other fault types can occur too
Normal faults are most expected, since the sinking slab pulls the crust apart
rationales: At trenches one plate goes under the other; sliding past is transform motion.
Thrust faults dominate, but the notes stress that other fault types can occur at subduction zones too.
Correct. At subduction zones the fault you would most expect is reverse or thrust, but not always; other fault types can also occur there.
Convergent boundaries are mainly compressional, so reverse or thrust faults are the most expected.
questions.takeaway: Subduction zones are dominated by thrust faults but are not limited to them.

questions.stem: Why was Richter's original magnitude scale replaced for measuring earthquakes worldwide?
options: It was strictly valid only for certain frequency and distance ranges
It measured only the damage seen in buildings close to the source
It could only be applied to earthquakes that happened under the sea
It was not logarithmic, so very large earthquakes could not be ranked
rationales: Correct. Richter built the scale for southern California using local stations. As stations spread worldwide, it proved strictly valid only for certain frequency and distance ranges.
Richter's scale used the amplitude recorded by seismographs, not observed damage. Damage-based measures are intensity scales.
The scale was developed for earthquakes in southern California, on land. Being limited to the sea was not its problem.
Richter's scale was logarithmic. The moment magnitude scale that replaced it is logarithmic too.
questions.takeaway: The Richter scale only worked for certain frequency and distance ranges, so moment magnitude replaced it.

questions.stem: Two earthquakes occur on faults in similar rock. Fault A ruptures a longer, wider area and slips further than fault B. What follows?
options: Fault B has the larger seismic moment, as less slip concentrates its energy
Fault A has the larger seismic moment, so it has the larger moment magnitude
Both have the same moment magnitude, because the rock is similar on both faults
They cannot be compared until shaking intensity has been mapped in every town
rationales: Seismic moment grows with slip and rupture area. Less slip means a smaller moment, not a concentrated one.
Correct. Seismic moment is rupture length × width × fault slip × shear modulus. With similar rock, the larger rupture and greater slip give fault A the larger moment and magnitude.
Similar rock fixes only the shear modulus. Rupture size and slip still differ, so the moments differ.
Moment magnitude comes from the rupture and seismic recordings, not from intensity maps.
questions.takeaway: Seismic moment = rupture length × width × slip × shear modulus; a bigger rupture with more slip means a bigger magnitude.

questions.stem: Two faults rupture identical areas with identical slip, but one is in rock that is far more resistant to deformation. Which has the larger seismic moment?
options: Neither, because seismic moment depends only on the rupture area and fault slip
The fault in less resistant rock, since weak rock lets slip release more energy
The fault in more resistant rock, since seismic moment scales with shear modulus
Neither, because seismic moment depends on the distance to the nearest station
rationales: Rupture area and slip matter, but the shear modulus is also part of the seismic moment.
The shear modulus multiplies the moment, so weaker rock gives a smaller moment for the same rupture.
Correct. Seismic moment includes the shear modulus, a measure of how resistant the rock is to deformation. With area and slip equal, the stiffer rock gives the larger moment.
Seismic moment describes the source itself. It does not depend on where stations happen to be.
questions.takeaway: Seismic moment includes the shear modulus, so rock stiffness matters as well as rupture size and slip.

questions.stem: What does the moment magnitude scale fundamentally reflect?
options: The amplitude of shaking recorded at the seismograph nearest the source
The energy spent moving large masses of rock on each side of the fault
The damage observed in buildings standing closest to the epicentre
The length of time shaking was felt by people at a fixed distance away
rationales: Amplitude at a local station was the basis of Richter's scale, which is no longer used.
Correct. Moment magnitude is based on the seismic moment, which relates to the energy expended moving rock on each side of the fault. The w stands for work.
Damage describes shaking intensity at a place, not the size of the earthquake.
Duration of felt shaking varies with location and does not define magnitude.
questions.takeaway: Moment magnitude (Mw) measures the work done moving rock during rupture.

questions.stem: Which statement follows from the Gutenberg–Richter law?
options: Big earthquakes are more common than small ones, since strain builds over time
Small earthquakes occur only in the years that lead up to a big earthquake
Earthquakes of every magnitude occur at about the same rate within a given region
Small earthquakes are very common, moderately large ones fewer, and big ones rare
rationales: This reverses the relationship. Larger earthquakes are much rarer.
Small earthquakes happen all the time, not only before large ones.
Frequency changes strongly with magnitude; that relationship is exactly what the law describes.
Correct. The Gutenberg–Richter law describes a power-law relationship: many small earthquakes, fewer moderately large ones and very few big ones.
questions.takeaway: Gutenberg–Richter: the bigger the magnitude, the rarer the earthquake.

questions.stem: An earthquake of magnitude 7 is compared with one of magnitude 5. Roughly how much more energy does the larger one release?
options: About 1,000 times more
About 100 times more
About 64 times more
About 20 times more
rationales: Correct. Each whole-number increase is about 32 times more energy, so two steps give about 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 times.
This assumes energy rises 10 times per step. The notes give about 32 times per step, so two steps is about 1,000 times.
This doubles 32 instead of multiplying it by itself. Energy grows by a factor of about 32 for each step.
This treats the steps as adding energy rather than multiplying it.
questions.takeaway: Each magnitude step is about 32× energy, so two steps is about 1,000×.

questions.stem: Each whole-number increase in magnitude releases about 32 times more energy. About how many magnitude 6 earthquakes release the same energy as a single magnitude 7?
options: Roughly 1,000 of them
Roughly 32 of them
Roughly 10 of them
Roughly 7 of them
rationales: About 1,000 magnitude 6 events match a magnitude 8, which is two steps up, not one.
Correct. One magnitude step is a factor of about 32 in energy, so about 32 magnitude 6 events match one magnitude 7.
Ten per step is a tempting guess from the logarithmic scale, but energy rises about 32 times per step.
This has no basis in the energy relationship and ignores that each step multiplies energy.
questions.takeaway: One step up in magnitude is about 32 times the energy.

questions.stem: A fault zone produces many moderate earthquakes and, rarely, a very large one. Over the long term, which statement about the energy released is best supported?
options: Most energy is released in the few largest earthquakes, not the many small ones
Energy is shared equally, since frequency exactly balances the size of each event
Small earthquakes release enough energy to stop large ones from ever happening
Most energy comes from the many small earthquakes, since they are far more common
rationales: Correct. Energy rises so steeply with magnitude (about 32 times per step) that most of a fault's energy is released in a few of its largest earthquakes.
Frequency does not offset size. The energy increase per magnitude step outweighs the drop in frequency.
Small earthquakes do not release enough strain to rule out large ones.
Small events are more common, but each releases so little energy that together they do not match the rare large ones.
questions.takeaway: Most fault energy is released in the rare largest earthquakes.

questions.stem: News reports say an earthquake struck under a coastal town, but seismologists say the rupture began many kilometres below the ground. Which terms describe these two points?
options: The town sits above the hypocentre; the rupture began at the epicentre
The town sits on the wavefront; the rupture began at the fault scarp
The town sits above the epicentre; the rupture began at the hypocentre
The town sits on the fault scarp; the rupture began at the wavefront
rationales: This swaps the terms. The epicentre is on the surface, above the hypocentre.
A wavefront moves out from the source, and a fault scarp is on the surface. Neither marks where the rupture began.
Correct. The hypocentre (focus) is where the earthquake originates, and the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.
A fault scarp is a landform made by surface offset, and a wavefront is a surface of equal travel time. Neither is the origin point.
questions.takeaway: Hypocentre = where the rupture starts; epicentre = the point on the surface above it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly separates earthquake magnitude from shaking intensity?
options: Magnitude and intensity both vary by place, but only intensity uses a logarithmic scale
Magnitude varies by place and observed damage; intensity is one value from seismic records
Magnitude and intensity are both single values, calculated from the same seismic recordings
Magnitude is one value from seismic records; intensity varies by place and observed damage
rationales: Magnitude does not vary by place, and it is the moment magnitude scale that is logarithmic.
This swaps the two. Magnitude is the single value; intensity varies from place to place.
Intensity is not a single value; it changes from place to place and comes from observations.

Correct. Magnitude measures energy released and is one value per earthquake, calculated from seismic recordings. Intensity is the strength of shaking at a location, judged from observed shaking and damage.
questions.takeaway: Magnitude: one value, energy, from recordings. Intensity: varies by place, from shaking and damage.

questions.stem: After an earthquake, a team gathers shaking reports and damage observations town by town and grades each location. What are they producing?
options: A seismic hazard map, giving the shaking expected over the coming decades
A moment magnitude estimate, calculated from the seismic moment of the fault
An intensity map, such as one using the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale
A Gutenberg–Richter plot, comparing how often each magnitude level occurs
rationales: A hazard map forecasts future shaking probabilities; this team is recording what one past earthquake did.
Moment magnitude is one value from seismic recordings, not a town-by-town grade from observations.
Correct. Intensity is determined from observed shaking and damage and varies from place to place, which is what the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale records.
A Gutenberg–Richter plot uses many earthquakes' magnitudes, not damage reports from one event.
questions.takeaway: Grading observed shaking and damage place by place produces an intensity map (e.g. MMI).

questions.stem: During an earthquake, one mid-rise building sways violently while shorter and taller buildings nearby shake far less. What best explains this?
options: The building stood nearer the epicentre, since intensity changes over short distances
The seismic waves' frequency was close to the building's natural frequency
The building received larger P waves, which mainly affect medium-height structures
The building had the greatest mass, and heavier buildings always shake the hardest
rationales: The buildings are next to each other, so distance from the epicentre is effectively the same.
Correct. Buildings shake more strongly when the frequency of the seismic waves is close to their natural frequency, which amplifies the motion. That is resonance.
P waves have smaller amplitude, and they do not single out buildings of a particular height.
Mass alone does not decide how much a building shakes; the match between wave and building frequency does.
questions.takeaway: Resonance: buildings shake hardest when wave frequency matches their natural frequency.

questions.stem: Two towns lie the same distance from an earthquake. One is built on hard rock; the other sits on a sedimentary basin of soft ground. What is expected?
options: Shaking is stronger and lasts longer in the basin town, as soft ground amplifies it
Shaking is weaker in the basin town, because soft ground absorbs the seismic energy
Shaking is stronger on hard rock, since seismic waves travel faster through solid rock
Shaking is the same in both, since intensity depends only on distance from the source
rationales: Correct. Sedimentary basins or soft ground amplify ground motion, increasing both its strength and duration through basin resonance, even far from the source.
Soft ground amplifies shaking rather than absorbing it.
Faster travel does not mean stronger shaking. Soft ground is where amplification happens.
Distance matters, but local ground conditions also control shaking at a site.
questions.takeaway: Soft ground and sedimentary basins amplify shaking in strength and duration.

questions.stem: In general, how does shaking intensity change with distance from an earthquake's source?
options: It stays the same at every distance for an earthquake of a given size
It is weakest near the source and builds up the further away you are
It is greatest at one set distance where the waves first come together
It is greatest near the source and generally weakens with distance
rationales: Intensity varies from place to place. That is one of the ways it differs from magnitude.
This reverses the general pattern. Intensity usually drops as the waves travel.
There is no fixed distance of peak shaking. Shaking generally decreases away from the source.
Correct. Shaking intensity is generally greatest near the source and attenuates, or dissipates, with distance.
questions.takeaway: Shaking intensity generally decreases with distance from the source.

questions.stem: A city far from an earthquake suffers severe damage, while towns much nearer the source escape lightly. Which set of factors from the notes could explain this?
options: Soft basin ground, buildings resonating with the waves, and the rupture's direction
Faster P waves, shorter shaking and the city's distance from any plate boundary
A smaller magnitude, a deeper hypocentre and fewer aftershocks near the city
Hard bedrock, shorter buildings and a rupture travelling away from the city
rationales: Correct. Soft soil, resonance and directivity (the direction the rupture travels) can all raise shaking far from the source.
P waves are less destructive, shorter shaking reduces damage, and plate-boundary distance does not raise local shaking.
A smaller or deeper earthquake would weaken shaking everywhere, and aftershocks do not explain a distant city's damage.
Each of these would reduce shaking in the city rather than increase it.
questions.takeaway: Site effects (soft ground, resonance) and rupture directivity can make distant places shake hardest.

questions.stem: Compared with a smaller earthquake, what does a larger magnitude earthquake generally produce?
options: Weaker shaking, as its energy spreads further out
Stronger maximum shaking that is over more quickly
Stronger maximum shaking that also lasts for longer
The same maximum shaking spread over a wider area
rationales: Larger earthquakes release more energy, so shaking is stronger, not weaker.
Larger earthquakes rupture longer faults, so shaking lasts longer, not shorter.
Correct. Maximum shaking and its duration both scale roughly with magnitude.
Larger earthquakes produce stronger maximum shaking as well as affecting a wider area.
questions.takeaway: Bigger earthquakes shake harder and longer.

questions.stem: An earthquake within very old, unbroken rock in the middle of a plate is felt unusually far away. Why?
options: Old rock sits on plate boundaries, where the largest earthquakes take place
Old rock produces only surface waves, which never lose energy with distance
Old rock is softer, so it amplifies shaking in the same way as a basin does
Seismic waves travel further without weakening through old, unbroken rock
rationales: These earthquakes are intraplate: they happen away from plate boundaries.
Earthquakes in old rock still produce body and surface waves, and all waves weaken with distance.
Old cratonic rock is hard and unbroken, not soft basin sediment.
Correct. Old cratonic rock is not easily broken, so seismic waves travel further through it without weakening.
questions.takeaway: Waves travel far through old, unbroken rock, so intraplate quakes there can be felt over wide areas.

questions.stem: Which earthquake is best described as intraplate?
options: One triggered by human activity, such as injecting wastewater underground
One that occurs within a tectonic plate, well away from its boundaries
One that occurs where two plates slide past each other along a transform
One that occurs where two plates collide at a subduction zone trench
rationales: Earthquakes triggered by human activity are classed as induced seismicity, whatever their location.
Correct. Intraplate earthquakes occur within a tectonic plate, away from its boundaries.
Transform earthquakes occur at a plate boundary.
Subduction zone earthquakes are plate-boundary earthquakes.
questions.takeaway: Intraplate = within a plate, away from boundaries; induced = triggered by human activity.

questions.stem: A region with long-inactive faults begins to have earthquakes after large volumes of wastewater are injected underground. What is the mechanism?
options: Injected fluid raises underground pressure, letting existing faults slip
The water cools the rock, which shrinks and cracks along brand-new faults
The added weight of water pushes the crust down and creates new faults
Injection heats the faults, melting the rock until it flows and ruptures
rationales: Correct. Injecting large volumes of water increases underground fluid pressure, which can cause existing, previously inactive faults to slip.
Cooling and shrinking is not the mechanism; the notes point to increased fluid pressure on existing faults.
The mechanism is fluid pressure on existing faults, not the weight of the water making new ones.
The rock does not melt. Higher fluid pressure lets faults slip.
questions.takeaway: Induced seismicity: raised fluid pressure lets existing faults slip.

questions.stem: Two countries experience similar earthquakes. The first records larger economic losses but few deaths; the second records smaller economic losses but many deaths. What best explains this?
options: The first has mostly intraplate earthquakes; the second has mostly plate-boundary earthquakes
The first has more valuable exposed assets but safer buildings; the second has weaker buildings
The first has stronger earthquakes overall; the second has more frequent but smaller earthquakes
The first sits on hard rock everywhere; the second sits entirely on soft sedimentary basins
rationales: The type of earthquake does not explain why one country loses more money but fewer lives.

Correct. Comparing rich and poor countries, the notes show a contrast between economic and life losses. Costly assets drive economic loss, while weak buildings drive deaths: earthquakes don't kill, buildings kill.
The stem says the earthquakes are similar, so the difference lies in exposure and vulnerability.
Ground conditions matter, but they would not neatly split economic losses from deaths. Building quality and wealth explain the pattern.
questions.takeaway: Wealth raises economic losses; weak buildings raise deaths. Buildings, not earthquakes, kill.

questions.stem: A country has strong earthquake building codes, yet many recently built buildings collapse in an earthquake. Which explanation fits the notes?
options: Strong codes make buildings stiff, which always worsens resonance damage
Codes guard only against P waves, so the later S waves caused the collapses
The codes were laxly enforced, so buildings did not meet the standard set
Building codes cover only tall buildings, so low-rise housing was unprotected
rationales: Codes are designed to reduce damage; resonance depends on the match between wave and building frequency.
Codes are not written for one wave type. The failures came from buildings not meeting the code.
Correct. The notes contrast strong building codes with often lax enforcement. A code only helps if buildings are actually built to it.
Nothing in the notes limits codes to tall buildings. The issue highlighted is enforcement.
questions.takeaway: Building codes reduce losses only when they are enforced.

questions.stem: Which pairing correctly matches each term to an example?
options: Hazard: the quality of local buildings; exposure: the ground shaking expected
Hazard: the people and buildings in its path; exposure: the ground shaking expected
Hazard: the ground shaking expected; exposure: the quality of local buildings
Hazard: the ground shaking expected; exposure: the people and buildings in its path
rationales: Building quality relates to vulnerability, not hazard, and shaking is the hazard rather than exposure.
This swaps hazard and exposure.
Shaking is the hazard, but building quality is vulnerability. Exposure is who and what is in the path.
Correct. A seismic hazard map shows expected ground shaking, while exposure models are based on the buildings and population in harm's way.
questions.takeaway: Hazard = the shaking; exposure = people and buildings in its path; vulnerability = how badly they fare.

questions.stem: A seismic hazard map shows high expected shaking in a remote mountain range, yet a map of expected losses ranks the same area low. Why?
options: Hazard maps exaggerate remote areas, where fewer seismometers are installed
Few people or buildings are exposed there, so expected losses stay small
Mountains amplify shaking less than basins, so the hazard has been overstated
Loss maps ignore ground shaking and count only past deaths in each area
rationales: Nothing suggests the hazard is wrong. The difference comes from exposure.
Correct. Loss depends on hazard, exposure and vulnerability together. High hazard with little exposure means low expected loss.
The stem gives no reason to doubt the hazard map. Low loss follows from low exposure.
Loss models combine ground shaking with exposure and vulnerability; they do not ignore shaking.
questions.takeaway: High hazard does not mean high loss without exposure and vulnerability.

questions.stem: Which event is most likely to generate a tsunami?
options: A thrust fault that suddenly uplifts a large area of the seafloor
A strike-slip fault that moves two blocks of seafloor sideways
A deep earthquake beneath a continent, far from any coastline
A strong storm wind blowing steadily over the open ocean
rationales: Correct. A tsunami is caused by sudden displacement of a large volume of water. Reverse (thrust) faults usually cause earthquake tsunamis by uplifting or lowering a large area of seafloor.
Sideways motion displaces little water vertically, so it is much less effective at generating a tsunami.
An earthquake beneath a continent does not displace seawater.
Wind makes regular wind-driven waves, not a tsunami.
questions.takeaway: Tsunamis need sudden displacement of a large volume of water, typically by thrust faulting of the seafloor.

questions.stem: A tsunami crosses a deep ocean basin and then a broad, shallow continental shelf. Where is it fastest, and where is it tallest?
options: Fastest over the shallow shelf; tallest out over the deep ocean basin
